statement: Unit testing is the basis of Test-Driven Development (TDD): a failing test is written first, code is written to satisfy the test, and then code quality is improved by refactoring.

Combining production code with testing logic (e.g. print statements used for unit testing) is not good practice: it increases code complexity, degrades readability, increases execution time, and can cause the production code to malfunction if misconfigured.

Unit test classes should be placed in the same package as the source class under test (e.g., org.packt.BarTest for org.packt.Bar) but in a separate source folder (src/ vs test/), so that the test code can access protected and default members without being bundled in production artifacts.

A test suite takes time to execute when individual tests perform integration tasks such as acquiring a database connection, connecting to the Internet, interacting with an SMTP server, or performing file I/O; these are integration tests, not unit tests.

When a test suite takes hours to execute it blocks the progress of development and defeats the purpose of quick feedback in TDD; each test in TDD should not take more than a few milliseconds to execute.

Unit tests mock external dependencies using test doubles so they execute very quickly; Mockito provides APIs to mock a database connection or SMTP connection so the actual logic can be unit tested in isolation from external resources.

When unit tests interact with the real database and Internet connection, chances of test failure increase because the database state might not be the same across all test runs and each Internet call might return different values, making assertions on constant values unreliable.
The org.mockito.Mockito.mock() static method creates mock proxy objects; alternatively, the @Mock annotation can be used to annotate field declarations in the test class.

When using @Mock annotations, mocks must be initialized before test execution: either by calling MockitoAnnotations.initMocks(this) in a @Before method, or by annotating the test class with @RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class).
Mockito cannot mock or spy on final classes and methods, static methods, enums, private methods, the equals() and hashCode() methods, primitive types, and anonymous classes.

PowerMockito (an extension of the Mockito framework) can overcome Mockito's limitations and mock static and private methods; however, mocking private or static properties violates encapsulation, and the preferred approach is to refactor the offending code to make it testable.
If a method of a mock object is not stubbed, the mock returns default values: false for Boolean return types, null for object return types, and 0 for integer or long return types.

Mockito.when() identifies a method to stub and thenReturn() specifies the value to return; together, when(mock.method(matcher)).thenReturn(value) stubs a method to return a specific value for a given input.

Mockito provides four stubbing action methods: thenReturn(value) to return a specific value; thenThrow(throwable) to throw a specific exception; thenAnswer(answer) to execute custom logic and return a computed value; thenCallRealMethod() to invoke the real method.

void methods are auto-stubbed on mock objects and do not connect to the real implementation; because void methods return nothing, the verify() method must be used to assert that the void method was called with the expected arguments.
verify(mock).method(args) verifies that a method was called on a mock object; if the method was not invoked by the code under test, verify() raises an exception indicating a bug.

verify() supports the following invocation-count modes: times(n) — exactly n invocations; never() — zero invocations; atLeastOnce() — at least one invocation; atLeast(n) — at least n invocations; atMost(n) — at most n invocations; only() — the only method called on the mock; timeout(millis) — interaction within a time bound.
verifyZeroInteractions(mocks...) verifies that no methods were called on the given mock objects at all; it is useful for asserting that a code path does not interact with a particular collaborator.
verifyNoMoreInteractions(mocks...) checks that no unverified interactions remain on the given mocks after all expected verify() calls have been made, guarding against unexpected extra method calls.

To throw an exception from a non-void stubbed method use when(mock.method(args)).thenThrow(exception); to throw an exception from a void stubbed method use the syntax doThrow(exception).when(mock).voidMethod(args).

To unit test a Spring MVC controller in isolation from the servlet container, create a @Mock for each service dependency, instantiate the controller directly in @Before setup, and inject the mock via the controller's setter method, then run with MockitoJUnitRunner.

Each controller unit test method should cover exactly one scenario (e.g., invalid login vs. valid login) and stub the mock service to return the appropriate value for that scenario before invoking the controller method under test.

To unit test a Spring service layer, create a @Mock for the DAO interface dependency, instantiate the service in @Before setup, and inject the mock DAO via the service's setter; the service can then be tested without a real database.
When a service calls a DAO void method (e.g., create()), stub it to throw a runtime exception with doThrow().when(dao).create(...) to test error-handling branches without a real database.

To unit test a Spring DAO class (e.g., RegistrationDaoSpring), mock JdbcTemplate with @Mock JdbcTemplate, construct the DAO with the mock template in @Before setup, and use ArgumentCaptor to verify that SQL parameters are passed in the correct order.

ArgumentCaptor.forClass(T.class) captures arguments passed to a stubbed method on a mock; after verify() with captor.capture(), calling captor.getAllValues() returns the captured arguments in invocation order, enabling assertion of argument sequencing.

Integration tests that query a real database or send real e-mail are explicitly distinguished from unit tests; unit tests mock all external dependencies, while integration tests verify end-to-end application and database integrity.

Spring integration tests that must not corrupt the development database should be annotated with @Transactional at the class level and @TransactionConfiguration(transactionManager = "...", defaultRollback = true) to automatically roll back all transactions after each test.

@RunWith(SpringJUnit4ClassRunner.class) enables a test class to benefit from Spring's TestContext framework features (application context loading, dependency injection, transaction support); it cannot be combined with @RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class).
The @ContextConfiguration annotation specifies the resource locations (XML files) or annotated @Configuration classes from which the Spring ApplicationContext is loaded for integration tests.

Spring 3.1 profiles allow different sets of beans to be loaded for different environments (dev, prod, test); the @ActiveProfiles annotation on a test class instructs the container which named profile(s) to activate during context loading.
Beans defined without a profile name are always loaded regardless of which active profile is specified; beans defined under a profile name are only loaded when that profile is active.

MockEnvironment and MockPropertySource (added in Spring 3.2) allow property values to be overridden in tests without reading the real properties file; they are applied via an ApplicationContextInitializer passed to @ContextConfiguration(initializers = ...).

A JNDI lookup defined via <jee:jndi-lookup> can be mocked in out-of-container tests by using SimpleNamingContextBuilder inside an ApplicationContextInitializer to bind a Mockito mock object to the JNDI name before the context is loaded.

ReflectionTestUtils provides reflection-based utility methods to access private fields and invoke private/protected setter methods in Spring beans under test, accommodating JPA/Hibernate entities that use field-level access and Spring's @Autowired private-field injection.

MockMvc allows Spring MVC controllers to be tested by performing actual HTTP requests and verifying response status codes and response body content (e.g., JSON paths) without spinning up a real servlet container.
To build a MockMvc instance, annotate the test class with @WebAppConfiguration, autowire WebApplicationContext, and call MockMvcBuilders.webAppContextSetup(wac).build() in a @Before method.

Spring's TestContext framework is an annotation-driven framework that follows the convention-over-configuration design paradigm; it provides dependency injection, transaction management, and context caching for JUnit and TestNG test classes without requiring them to extend a framework class.

When a custom TestExecutionListener is registered via @TestExecutionListeners, the default listeners are not registered automatically; the developer must explicitly re-declare all default listeners or use mergeMode = MergeMode.MERGE_WITH_DEFAULTS to merge custom and default listeners.

The @DirtiesContext annotation marks an ApplicationContext as dirtied (modified) during a test; the framework removes it from the context cache and closes it so subsequent tests start with a fresh context.

In a layered Spring web application, unit tests for each layer (web, service, DAO) should be independent: the web layer test mocks the service, the service test mocks the DAO interface, and the DAO test mocks JdbcTemplate — no layer's test starts the real implementation of another layer.

A DAO interface (e.g., RegistrationDao) should be introduced between the service layer and the data access implementation so that the service can be unit tested by mocking the interface; without an interface Mockito cannot isolate the service from the database.

Request-scoped and session-scoped Spring beans can be tested with @WebAppConfiguration by autowiring MockHttpServletRequest and MockHttpSession; setting request parameters and session attributes on these mocks makes the scoped beans return the expected test data.
Automated unit tests provide a quick regression safety net for refactoring and new features; they reduce over-engineering because code is written only to satisfy a failing test.

JUnit 4 is annotation-based and non-invasive: test classes do not need to extend a framework class, any public method annotated with @Test becomes a test, and @Before/@After replace the older setUp/tearDown contract.
JUnit 4 enjoys better mocking support than TestNG, including a custom JUnit4 runner (MockitoJUnitRunner) from Mockito, which makes it the preferred framework for Mockito-based unit tests.

TestExecutionListener logic can be shared across multiple test class hierarchies and projects, unlike JUnit @Before/@After annotations which are test-class-specific and cannot be reused without class inheritance.

To achieve loose coupling enabling layer-specific changes (e.g., replacing Spring JDBC with Hibernate) without affecting other layers, a Spring web application should be divided into a data access layer, service layer, and controller layer.
